deck: BC habitat zones made simple
back: Biogeoclimatic ecosystem classification: how BC sorts land by climate, plants and soil.

deck: BC habitat zones made simple
front: Name the Interior zones from the valley floor up.
back: BG Bunchgrass, PP Ponderosa pine, IDF Interior Douglas fir, MS Montane spruce, ESSF Engelmann spruce and subalpine fir, AT Alpine tundra. Big Pines In Many Elk Areas.

deck: BC habitat zones made simple
back: IDF = Interior Douglas fir zone. x = very dry, h = hot. 2 = the local variant.

deck: BC habitat zones made simple
front: First small letter of a subzone: what does it tell you?
back: How wet: x very dry, d dry, m moist, w wet, v very wet.

deck: BC habitat zones made simple
front: Second small letter of an Interior subzone?
back: How warm: h hot, w warm, m mild, k cool, c cold.

deck: BC habitat zones made simple
back: It sits in the rain shadow of the Coast Mountains. Pacific air drops its rain on the coast side.

deck: BC habitat zones made simple
front: Rain and snow a year near Mission versus Kamloops?
back: About 2,140 mm at Haney (Maple Ridge) versus about 242 mm at Kamloops: about 9 times more.

deck: BC habitat zones made simple
front: Which zone gets the most snow?
back: ESSF: about 782 cm a year at Boss Mountain, with snowpack up to nearly 4 m.

deck: BC habitat zones made simple
front: What zone is Heffley Creek in?
back: PPxh2: Ponderosa pine, very dry hot (BC zone map, 2026-10-11).

deck: BC habitat zones made simple
back: CWHdm3: Coastal Western Hemlock, dry maritime.

deck: BC habitat zones made simple
front: Zones from Heffley Creek east to Sun Peaks?
back: PPxh2 valley, IDFxh2 and IDFdk2 slopes, MSdm3 plateau, ESSFdc3 at Sun Peaks. 4 zones in about 27 km.

deck: BC habitat zones made simple
front: Big tree key: open orange barked pine park?
back: PP, Ponderosa pine zone.

deck: BC habitat zones made simple
front: Big tree key: narrow spruce and fir spires, deep snow?
back: ESSF, Engelmann spruce and subalpine fir zone.

deck: BC habitat zones made simple
front: Big tree key: cedar and hemlock in the Interior?
back: ICH, Interior cedar and hemlock, the wet belt.

deck: BC habitat zones made simple
front: How does aspect change the zone?
back: South slopes act like a lower, hotter zone; north slopes act like a higher, cooler one.

deck: BC habitat zones made simple
front: How far can mule deer migrate to winter in the PP and IDF?
back: Up to about 80 km.

deck: BC habitat zones made simple
back: Deer struggle past about 30 cm. Moose move freely to about 40 cm, with slight difficulty at 40 to 70 cm.

deck: BC habitat zones made simple
back: Ecosystems with frequent stand maintaining fires: BG, PP and IDF. Ground fires kept them open.

deck: BC habitat zones made simple
front: The 5 steps to read a zone in the field?
back: Height and aspect, big trees, plants at your boots, moss and snow clues, confirm on the map.

deck: Grasslands
front: How much of BC is grassland?
back: Under 1% of the land, but about 30% of the province species at risk depend on it.

deck: Grasslands
back: Lower: sage, valley to about 700 m. Middle: no sage, 700 to 1,000 m. Upper: fescue, inside the IDF above about 900 m.

deck: Grasslands
front: Main grass of the Bunchgrass zone?
back: Bluebunch wheatgrass.

deck: Grasslands
back: More sagebrush, cheatgrass, prickly pear cactus and knapweed; less bunchgrass.

deck: Grasslands
front: Where are grassland deer in October at noon?
back: In brushy draws, on timber edges and near water. DEW: Draws, Edges, Water.

deck: Grasslands
front: How do you stalk a deer on open grass?
back: Use a draw or fold below the skyline, wind in your face, move when its head is down.

deck: Grasslands
front: Hunting a grazing lease with cattle on it?
back: Not without the consent of the lessee or occupant (synopsis page 9).

deck: Grasslands
back: Still subject to the Trespass Act (synopsis page 9).

deck: Grasslands
front: When are rattlesnakes back in their dens?
back: Virtually all by mid October. They come out in March and April.

deck: Grasslands
front: How far do rattlesnakes usually move from a den?
back: Seldom more than about 1.5 km.

deck: Grasslands
front: Who graze IDF grasslands in early spring?
back: Mule and white tailed deer.

deck: Grasslands
back: California quail, pheasant and chukar; gray partridge came from Washington.

deck: Grasslands
front: Why glass a basin at first light?
back: Deer are still on feed in the open, and you see far in grass country.

deck: Grasslands
back: A hillside behind the animal. Never a deer on the skyline.

deck: Grasslands
front: Cheatgrass risk for a quail dog?
back: Its seeds work into paws, ears and noses. Check the dog after every hunt (Tip).

deck: Grasslands
back: The lowest, driest grassland belt; a mule deer winter food.

deck: Dry forests: ponderosa pine and Douglas fir
back: 335 to 900 m; 280 to 500 mm a year. The driest, warmest forest zone.

deck: Dry forests: ponderosa pine and Douglas fir
back: About 350 to 1,450 m; 300 to 750 mm a year.

deck: Dry forests: ponderosa pine and Douglas fir
back: Mostly in 3s, 12 to 20 cm long.

deck: Dry forests: ponderosa pine and Douglas fir
back: In 2s, 2 to 7 cm long.

deck: Dry forests: ponderosa pine and Douglas fir
back: Single soft needles 2 to 3 cm; cones with 3 pointed bracts like mouse tails.

deck: Dry forests: ponderosa pine and Douglas fir
front: Why were dry pine forests open?
back: Frequent ground fires killed small trees and brush; thick barked old trees lived.

deck: Dry forests: ponderosa pine and Douglas fir
front: Mean fire interval at Trout Creek near Summerland, 1715 to 1952?
back: About 18 years.

deck: Dry forests: ponderosa pine and Douglas fir
back: Dense thickets of young trees filled in, cutting views and feed.

deck: Dry forests: ponderosa pine and Douglas fir
front: 3 jobs of old fir on winter range?
back: Catches snow, drops food (needles, lichen), and sits on a sunny south slope.

deck: Dry forests: ponderosa pine and Douglas fir
front: When do fir needles peak in Kamloops mule deer diet?
back: December and January.

deck: Dry forests: ponderosa pine and Douglas fir
back: Big sagebrush, pasture sage, bitterbrush, rabbitbrush, snowbrush, saskatoon, rose, serviceberry and Douglas fir.

deck: Dry forests: ponderosa pine and Douglas fir
front: Mule deer year in dry forest country?
back: Often high in September; moving down October and November; low PP and IDF south slopes December to March.

deck: Dry forests: ponderosa pine and Douglas fir
front: Ground plants of a dry IDF floor?
back: Bluebunch wheatgrass, kinnikinnick, soopolallie, spirea, saskatoon.

deck: Dry forests: ponderosa pine and Douglas fir
front: Midday in open dry forest: where are deer?
back: Bedded on benches, heads of draws, shady north edges, under big fir.

deck: Dry forests: ponderosa pine and Douglas fir
back: About 3 slow steps, then a long look. Look for parts: an ear, a leg.

deck: Dry forests: ponderosa pine and Douglas fir
back: Blue grouse.

deck: Wet forests and the coast
back: CWH, Coastal Western Hemlock: mean about 2,228 mm, range 1,000 to 4,400 mm.

deck: Wet forests and the coast
back: Western hemlock, western redcedar, coast Douglas fir; red alder on disturbed sites.

deck: Wet forests and the coast
back: Interior cedar and hemlock zone, the Interior wet belt: most productive Interior forest.

deck: Wet forests and the coast
front: Why is dense second growth poor deer feed?
back: In the pole stage, crowded trees overtop and shade out shrubs and herbs.

deck: Wet forests and the coast
front: How does old growth help coast deer in snow?
back: Crowns intercept snow, and broken branches and lichens give forage.

deck: Wet forests and the coast
back: Douglas fir, western redcedar, red huckleberry, salal, deer fern, tree lichens.

deck: Wet forests and the coast
front: Black tailed deer summer and fall foods?
back: Grasses, trailing blackberry, fireweed, pearly everlasting, forbs, and leaves of willow, salmonberry, salal and maple.

deck: Wet forests and the coast
front: Most common big mammals of the CWH?
back: Black tailed deer, black bear, grizzly bear, gray wolf.

deck: Wet forests and the coast
front: Where do coast black bears den?
back: Mostly in or under big trees, snags, logs or stumps.

deck: Wet forests and the coast
back: Leathery, sharply toothed, egg shaped evergreen leaves 3 to 9 cm; thickets.

deck: Wet forests and the coast
back: Stems armed with yellow spines 5 to 10 mm long. Do not grab it.

deck: Wet forests and the coast
front: Where to sit in thick coast cover at dusk?
back: On the edge where timber meets a cutblock or opening, wind to you.

deck: Wet forests and the coast
back: About November to early December.

deck: Wet forests and the coast
back: About 82 cm a year at the Haney station; it usually melts fast.

deck: Wet forests and the coast
front: Roosevelt elk on the coast eat?
back: Sedges, grasses, ferns, plus willow, elderberry, blueberry, cedar and hemlock browse.

deck: Wet forests and the coast
front: First check before any Mission area spot?
back: The Region 2 No Shooting areas in the Rule Book.

deck: Wetlands, marshes and riparian strips
back: Open water, marsh, fen, swamp, bog. Our Moose Feed in Swamps and Bogs.

deck: Wetlands, marshes and riparian strips
back: Under 2 m at midsummer, under 10% emergent plants.

deck: Wetlands, marshes and riparian strips
back: Flooded with nutrient rich water, over 10% cover of cattail, bulrush, sedges.

deck: Wetlands, marshes and riparian strips
back: Wooded wetland: 25% or more cover of trees or tall shrubs.

deck: Wetlands, marshes and riparian strips
back: Sphagnum moss peat fed by rain, acid; Labrador tea, bog cranberry, stunted spruce or pine.

deck: Wetlands, marshes and riparian strips
back: Peat over 40 cm fed by groundwater; sedges, willow, scrub birch.

deck: Wetlands, marshes and riparian strips
front: Who uses the willow edge of a marsh?
back: Moose and deer.

deck: Wetlands, marshes and riparian strips
back: Puddle ducks tip up in shallow water; divers dive in deeper water.

deck: Wetlands, marshes and riparian strips
back: Aquatic plants: horsetail, burweed, pondweeds.

deck: Wetlands, marshes and riparian strips
back: Willows first; red osier dogwood, cottonwood, birch, aspen, high bush cranberry.

deck: Wetlands, marshes and riparian strips
front: Riparian reserve on an S2 fish stream (5 to 20 m)?
back: 30 m reserve plus 20 m management zone each side (FPPR section 47).

deck: Wetlands, marshes and riparian strips
front: Riparian zones on an S4 stream (under 1.5 m)?
back: No reserve; 30 m management zone.

deck: Wetlands, marshes and riparian strips
front: Why are creek strips good in farm country?
back: They are hidden travel lanes from bed to feed.

deck: Wetlands, marshes and riparian strips
front: Beaver pond: what to look for?
back: Ducks on the water, moose in the willow regrowth, tracks in the mud.

deck: Wetlands, marshes and riparian strips
front: Who calves in riparian areas in the IDF?
back: Moose and mule deer.

deck: Wetlands, marshes and riparian strips
back: Wind and sun, use cover, glass the edges, plan the retrieve.

deck: Wetlands, marshes and riparian strips
back: Plan it before you shoot. Never swim for a bird.

deck: After fire: what a burn looks like year 1 to 20
back: Black, green, shrub, thicket.

deck: After fire: what a burn looks like year 1 to 20
back: Grass, herbs and fireweed under the snags. Elk and bears graze.

deck: After fire: what a burn looks like year 1 to 20
back: Shrubs and aspen root suckers: peak browse for deer and moose.

deck: After fire: what a burn looks like year 1 to 20
back: Dense young forest: hiding cover, less food.

deck: After fire: what a burn looks like year 1 to 20
front: Which seeds germinate in response to fire?
back: Snowbrush (ceanothus) and lodgepole pine.

deck: After fire: what a burn looks like year 1 to 20
front: How does aspen come back after fire?
back: Root suckers that quickly form a dense shrub layer.

deck: After fire: what a burn looks like year 1 to 20
back: Moose used low and medium severity patches, especially wet sites.

deck: After fire: what a burn looks like year 1 to 20
front: Elk use of a prescribed burn over time (Montana)?
back: Up in years 1 to 2, then back to normal over 3 to 10 years.

deck: After fire: what a burn looks like year 1 to 20
back: Most break or fall in the first 15 years; few in the first 5.

deck: After fire: what a burn looks like year 1 to 20
back: Danger trees, hidden hot ash pits, floods and debris flows, unstable slopes and rockfall.

deck: After fire: what a burn looks like year 1 to 20
front: How long can post fire risks last?
back: 2 years or more in severely burned areas.

deck: After fire: what a burn looks like year 1 to 20
back: Park and camp in the open, more than a tree length from any snag.

deck: After fire: what a burn looks like year 1 to 20
back: Area restrictions, possible season closures, and new fireguard roads.

deck: After fire: what a burn looks like year 1 to 20
front: Best place to hunt in a burn?
back: Edges between unburned islands and burned feed.

deck: After fire: what a burn looks like year 1 to 20
back: 271 fires, about 871,036 ha; parts of the moose hunt north of Highway 20 closed.

deck: Cutblocks and logging: age stages and what lives there
back: Sparse, herb, shrub, pole and sapling, young, mature, old.

deck: Cutblocks and logging: age stages and what lives there
back: Shrubs under 2 m; usually under 20 years.

deck: Cutblocks and logging: age stages and what lives there
back: Shrubs 2 to 10 m; under 40 years.

deck: Cutblocks and logging: age stages and what lives there
back: Trees over 10 m, densely stocked, overtopping shrubs; little food.

deck: Cutblocks and logging: age stages and what lives there
back: Generally 40 to 80 years.

deck: Cutblocks and logging: age stages and what lives there
back: Deer, in low shrubs.

deck: Cutblocks and logging: age stages and what lives there
front: Which cutblock ages did moose select in one BC study?
back: 10 to 30 years since cut; they avoided 0 to 9 and over 30.

deck: Cutblocks and logging: age stages and what lives there
front: Why do moose still need cover in logged country?
back: To hide from predators and hunters, for shade and for shelter in storms.

deck: Cutblocks and logging: age stages and what lives there
back: Logging creates forage that disappears once the canopy closes.

deck: Cutblocks and logging: age stages and what lives there
front: Age a block by tree height?
back: Knee about 3 to 5 years, head about 8 to 12, twice your height about 15 to 20, dark poles 25 plus (Tip).

deck: Cutblocks and logging: age stages and what lives there
front: Read a logged landscape on satellite images?
back: Brown is new, bright green is young feed, dark green is old timber.

deck: Cutblocks and logging: age stages and what lives there
front: Best stand spot near a cutblock?
back: The edge where a young block meets timber, downwind.

deck: Cutblocks and logging: age stages and what lives there
front: ATV on a Forest Service Road?
back: Valid driver's licence and at least $200,000 third party liability insurance.

deck: Cutblocks and logging: age stages and what lives there
back: $575; serious cases up to $100,000 and/or a year in jail.

deck: Cutblocks and logging: age stages and what lives there
front: Why worry about new logging roads in moose country?
back: More access can lead to over harvesting.

deck: Cutblocks and logging: age stages and what lives there
back: Bare, then shrubs and deer, then tall shrubs and moose, then dark poles.

deck: Farmland and orchards: Okanagan and Fraser Valley
back: Only with the consent of the owner, lessee or occupant (synopsis page 9).

deck: Farmland and orchards: Okanagan and Fraser Valley
back: No hunting or shooting within 100 m of a church, school, playground, regional park, dwelling or occupied farm or ranch building.

deck: Farmland and orchards: Okanagan and Fraser Valley
back: Yes. Get the owner's consent.

deck: Farmland and orchards: Okanagan and Fraser Valley
front: Where do deer enter a field?
back: The corner or gap nearest thick cover, often the same each night (lore).

deck: Farmland and orchards: Okanagan and Fraser Valley
front: What do deer and elk do to fruit trees?
back: Chew buds, spurs, shoots and leaves; antler rubbing breaks branches.

deck: Farmland and orchards: Okanagan and Fraser Valley
back: At least 2.4 m tall with 15 cm mesh, secured to the ground.

deck: Farmland and orchards: Okanagan and Fraser Valley
back: 1.5 to 2.1 m, 7 to 9 high tensile wires 20 to 30 cm apart.

deck: Farmland and orchards: Okanagan and Fraser Valley
front: Why are farms on old winter range?
back: Agriculture sits in low valleys and riparian areas that ungulates used in winter.

deck: Farmland and orchards: Okanagan and Fraser Valley
back: Alfalfa and clover.

deck: Farmland and orchards: Okanagan and Fraser Valley
back: About 60% of about 130 fields grazed to the soil by waterfowl.

deck: Farmland and orchards: Okanagan and Fraser Valley
front: Most common waterfowl in Delta field surveys?
back: Mallard, American wigeon and snow goose.

deck: Farmland and orchards: Okanagan and Fraser Valley
front: Migratory birds wintering on the Fraser estuary?
back: About 5 million.

deck: Farmland and orchards: Okanagan and Fraser Valley
back: Watch from public roads at dusk, mark the entry, find the owner, ask and follow their rules.

deck: Farmland and orchards: Okanagan and Fraser Valley
back: In person, in daylight, no firearm in sight.

deck: Farmland and orchards: Okanagan and Fraser Valley
back: Know every building, worker and road; never shoot toward roofs, roads or livestock; close gates.

deck: Browse plants: what deer and moose eat, and how to ID them
back: Twigs, buds and leaves of shrubs and trees.

deck: Browse plants: what deer and moose eat, and how to ID them
back: Evergreen or not, opposite or alternate, leaf shape and edge, stem colour and thorns, place and fruit.

deck: Browse plants: what deer and moose eat, and how to ID them
back: Red osier dogwood, Douglas maple, snowberry, soopolallie, falsebox, high bush cranberry.

deck: Browse plants: what deer and moose eat, and how to ID them
back: Maple, Ash, Dogwood, Caprifoliaceae, Horse chestnut: opposite leaved woody plants.

deck: Browse plants: what deer and moose eat, and how to ID them
back: Alternate oval leaves saw toothed mostly on the top half; purple berries with a white bloom.

deck: Browse plants: what deer and moose eat, and how to ID them
back: Wedge shaped leaves 1 to 2 cm with 3 teeth at the tip, grey woolly beneath; dry slopes.

deck: Browse plants: what deer and moose eat, and how to ID them
back: Opposite leaves with veins curving to the tip, white berries, bright red young stems; wet ground.

deck: Browse plants: what deer and moose eat, and how to ID them
back: Evergreen, glossy sticky leaves 5 to 10 cm with 3 strong veins; dry slopes and burns.

deck: Browse plants: what deer and moose eat, and how to ID them
back: Evergreen, small opposite leathery glossy toothed leaves 1 to 3 cm.

deck: Browse plants: what deer and moose eat, and how to ID them
back: Willows first; red osier dogwood, cottonwood, paper birch, aspen, high bush cranberry, falsebox, subalpine fir.

deck: Browse plants: what deer and moose eat, and how to ID them
back: To about 2.5 m, and they break stems down to reach higher tips.

deck: Browse plants: what deer and moose eat, and how to ID them
front: How much does a moose eat a day in winter?
back: Up to about 20 kg.

deck: Browse plants: what deer and moose eat, and how to ID them
back: Deer tear: ragged end. Hares cut clean at about 45 degrees.

deck: Browse plants: what deer and moose eat, and how to ID them
back: Deer to about 1.2 m, elk 1.5 to 1.8 m, moose 1.8 to 2.4 m.

deck: Browse plants: what deer and moose eat, and how to ID them
back: Snowberry: opposite, smooth edged. Saskatoon: alternate, toothed on the top half.

deck: Browse plants: what deer and moose eat, and how to ID them
back: Sedges, horsetail and willow in wetlands; bunchgrass, forbs, serviceberry and rose on uplands.

deck: Browse plants: what deer and moose eat, and how to ID them
front: Coast evergreen browse for black tails?
back: Salal, red huckleberry, cedar, Douglas fir, deer fern.

deck: Berries, seeds and mast: food for bears, grouse and deer by month
back: The fruit and nuts of trees and shrubs. In the Interior: berries, hips and conifer seed.

deck: Berries, seeds and mast: food for bears, grouse and deer by month
back: Valleys mid to late July; higher slopes in August.

deck: Berries, seeds and mast: food for bears, grouse and deer by month
back: August into September; high patches later.

deck: Berries, seeds and mast: food for bears, grouse and deer by month
front: Fruits that hang on into winter?
back: Snowberry, rose hips, kinnikinnick, high bush cranberry.

deck: Berries, seeds and mast: food for bears, grouse and deer by month
front: Why does fruit ripen in a wave?
back: Warm, low, sunny sites ripen first; high and shady sites later.

deck: Berries, seeds and mast: food for bears, grouse and deer by month
back: Up to about 20,000.

deck: Berries, seeds and mast: food for bears, grouse and deer by month
front: Huckleberries a fall bear needs a day?
back: About 55 kg (about 366 calories per kg).

deck: Berries, seeds and mast: food for bears, grouse and deer by month
back: Spring green plants and newborn calves; summer insects, berries, carrion; fall berries and spawning fish.

deck: Berries, seeds and mast: food for bears, grouse and deer by month
back: Buds and catkins of aspen, poplar, birch and alder.

deck: Berries, seeds and mast: food for bears, grouse and deer by month
back: Pine and spruce needles, up in the trees.

deck: Berries, seeds and mast: food for bears, grouse and deer by month
back: Berries, clover, leaves and seeds; road edges at dawn.

deck: Berries, seeds and mast: food for bears, grouse and deer by month
back: Bright red bitter berries, soapy when crushed; leaves scaly underneath.

deck: Berries, seeds and mast: food for bears, grouse and deer by month
back: Shrub to 1.5 m, finely toothed leaves, purple berries 7 to 10 mm; ESSF.

deck: Berries, seeds and mast: food for bears, grouse and deer by month
back: Clark's nutcracker, red crossbill, pygmy nuthatch, squirrels.

deck: Berries, seeds and mast: food for bears, grouse and deer by month
back: There is no open season for grizzly bears in BC.

deck: Berries, seeds and mast: food for bears, grouse and deer by month
front: Sign a berry patch is in use?
back: Fresh seedy scat, broken branches, tracks.
